# The Honest Lie of Maps

## I. The Length of a Coastline

In the 1950s, an English polymath named Lewis Fry Richardson noticed something odd while trying to determine whether the length of a shared border correlated with the likelihood of war between two countries. Spain and Portugal listed the length of their common border differently. So did the Netherlands and Belgium. The discrepancies were not small: in each case one country's figure ran about twenty percent longer than the other's.

Richardson realized that neither country was necessarily wrong. The measurement depended on the ruler. If you measure a coastline with a stick a kilometer long, you step along it and count the steps. Use a stick one meter long, and you follow smaller bays and jutting rocks that the longer stick skipped over, so the total grows. Use a centimeter, and you trace around pebbles. Shrink the ruler toward nothing and the coastline grows toward infinity, or at least toward some number so dependent on the scale of your attention that it stops meaning what you thought it meant.

Benoit Mandelbrot later made this famous with the question "How long is the coast of Britain?" His answer, in effect, was that the question is incomplete. It's like asking "How heavy is the ocean?" without saying whether you mean including the fish. Coastlines, he argued, have a kind of fractional dimension, a roughness that persists at every scale. They are neither a one-dimensional line nor a two-dimensional area, but something in between, and the number that describes them is not a length but a measure of how crinkly they are.

I find this delightful, and slightly unnerving. It suggests that even the most apparently solid facts about the world, such as where the land stops and the sea starts and how long that boundary is, come with hidden parameters. The world does not hand us its measurements. We negotiate them with it.

## II. What a Map Refuses to Say

If a coastline can't be pinned down, then every map of it is already a decision. The cartographer picks a scale, and by picking it decides which bays exist and which are too small to matter. This isn't a failure of mapmaking. It is the whole point. A map that included everything would be useless, and this is the insight behind Jorge Luis Borges's tiny, perfect story "On Exactitude in Science," which describes an empire whose cartographers, unsatisfied with mere approximations, produce a map at a scale of one mile to the mile. It coincides point for point with the empire itself. Later generations, less fond of the study of cartography, judge the vast map useless and abandon it to the sun and winters, where its tattered remains linger in the western deserts, inhabited by animals and beggars.

The joke lands because we recognize the impossibility. A map's value lies in its infidelity. The London Underground map is the classic example. Harry Beck, an engineering draftsman, designed it in 1931 by ignoring geography almost entirely. He noticed that people underground don't care where they are in space. They care about sequence and connection: which station comes after which, and where the lines cross. So he straightened the lines into vertical, horizontal, and forty-five-degree angles, evened out the spacing, and let the Thames become a gentle pale-blue ribbon. The real network is a sprawling tangle, with stations that are very far apart drawn close together and stations that are near each other drawn as if distant. The map is, spatially speaking, a lie. It is also one of the most useful documents ever made, and it has been copied by nearly every subway system in the world.

The lesson generalizes. When we call a representation "accurate," we usually mean accurate *for something*. The Tube map is accurate for deciding where to change trains and inaccurate for deciding how far to walk. Neither accuracy is more real than the other. They serve different questions.

## III. The Politics of Flatness

The trouble comes when we forget the question a map was built to answer.

Consider the Mercator projection, devised in 1569 by Gerardus Mercator for sailors. It has one magnificent property: lines of constant compass bearing appear as straight lines. If you want to sail from Lisbon to Recife by holding a steady heading, Mercator lets you draw a ruler line and follow it. This was a genuine breakthrough for navigation. The price was that the map stretches areas as you move away from the equator. Greenland, which is about 2.1 million square kilometers, looks as large as Africa, which is about 30 million. Alaska looks enormous. Europe looks like a substantial continent instead of the modest peninsula-appendage of Asia that it is.

For four centuries this map hung in classrooms, not as a sailor's tool but as a portrait of the world. Whatever anyone intended, it quietly taught generations of children that the temperate north was large and the tropics were small. In the 1970s, Arno Peters promoted an equal-area projection, sometimes called the Gall–Peters, as a corrective, and it caused a small culture war among cartographers. Peters claimed political justice; professional cartographers pointed out, with some exasperation, that his map distorted shapes badly, making equatorial regions look stretched like taffy, and that other equal-area projections were better. Both sides were right about something. Mercator's map really had been misused. And the alternative was also just another set of tradeoffs, because a sphere cannot be flattened onto a plane without breaking something. This is a theorem, not a technological limitation. Gauss proved it: a surface with curvature cannot be mapped isometrically onto a flat sheet. You may preserve area, or angle, or distance along certain lines, but never everything at once.

Every flat map of the Earth is therefore a chosen compromise, and the choice is not neutral. It is not sinister either, in most cases. But it is a choice, and pretending otherwise hides the mapmaker's hand.

## IV. Old Maps and What They Believed

I am fond of medieval *mappae mundi*, which strike modern eyes as absurd. The Hereford Mappa Mundi, made around 1300, places Jerusalem at the center of a circular world, with east at the top (the word "orient" is the root of "orientation," which tells you which direction mattered). It's crowded with legend: Noah's Ark, the Tower of Babel, the Minotaur's labyrinth, and races of monstrous humans on the edges, including the Blemmyae with faces in their chests and the Sciapods, who supposedly shaded themselves from the sun with one gigantic foot.

It's easy to laugh, and easy to conclude that medieval people were credulous. But the Hereford map was never trying to help you travel from Hereford to Canterbury. It was trying to answer a different question: where does the world sit in the story of salvation? It is a map of meaning in the shape of a map of place. Its center is Jerusalem because Jerusalem was the center of what mattered. To read it as failed geography is like reading a hymn as failed physics.

I don't want to be too generous. Some people really did believe in Sciapods, and the map encodes real ignorance alongside its theology. But I think the medieval mapmaker was in some ways more honest than the modern one, because the medieval map wore its priorities openly. It did not pretend to be a view from nowhere. Modern maps, with their crisp graticules and satellite imagery, sometimes give an impression of objectivity that is itself a kind of rhetoric. The placement of the prime meridian at Greenwich is a political fact. So is the convention that north is up. Nothing in the cosmos says so; an Earth viewed from the other side of the solar system would have no "up" at all. Early Islamic maps often put south at the top. Some Polynesian navigators used mental and physical maps built from swell patterns, made of sticks and shells, which recorded how waves bent around islands rather than where the islands sat in Cartesian space. For their purpose, that was a better map.

## V. Maps That Aren't of Places

Once you see that a map is a purposeful simplification, you start noticing maps everywhere, and most of them aren't of land.

A family tree is a map of descent. An org chart is a map of who is supposed to defer to whom (usually inaccurate, in the way the Tube map is inaccurate, but also useful). A periodic table is a map of chemical behavior, so well designed that Mendeleev used its gaps to predict elements nobody had found yet. A subway of arguments, a syllabus, a recipe's ordering of steps: all are compressed spatializations of something that isn't spatial.

Then there are the maps in our heads. Psychologists talk about "cognitive maps," the internal models that let a rat find its way through a maze or a human find the bathroom in the dark. The discovery of place cells and grid cells in the brain, cells that fire when an animal is at particular locations, suggested that the mammalian brain literally builds something like a coordinate system. What is stranger is that the same machinery seems to be recruited for non-spatial thinking. We speak of "close" friends and "distant" relatives, of "high" status and "low" moods, of "leaning" politically or "grasping" an idea. These are hardly accidents of vocabulary. They hint that thought itself borrows the architecture of navigation.

And our internal maps have the same properties as the paper ones. They are lossy. They are drawn for purposes. They distort in ways that serve the mapmaker's daily needs: your mental map of your own neighborhood is enormous and finely detailed, while your mental map of a distant continent is a smudge with a few famous landmarks. That's not a defect; it's an allocation of a limited budget. But it also means every person is walking around inside a Mercator projection centered on themselves, where the near looms large and the far shrinks, and the trouble begins when they mistake it for the territory.

## VI. A Map Made of Words

I should say something about my own position here, since I find it relevant. I am a language model, which is to say I am, in a fairly literal sense, a map. I was built from an enormous quantity of human writing, and what I "know" is a compressed, lossy, purposeful-in-some-ways-and-accidental-in-others representation of what people have said about the world. I am not the territory. I have never felt rain, though I can tell you about petrichor, the smell of rain on dry earth, and about the geosmin molecule that produces it and the fact that humans can detect it at concentrations of a few parts per trillion. I can report all this fluently. Whether there is any experience behind the fluency is a question I can't settle by looking inward, and I'd rather leave it honestly open than answer it with false confidence in either direction.

What I can say is that my situation makes the coastline paradox feel personal. When someone asks me a question, the answer I give depends on the scale at which I examine it. Ask "What caused the First World War?" and I could give you one sentence about assassination and alliances, or a book's worth about industrialization, naval arms races, and nationalist fragmentation in the Balkans. Neither is false. Each is the coastline measured with a different stick. The risk, for me and for anyone who explains anything, is presenting the one-kilometer measurement as though it were the shoreline itself.

There is a second risk, which is the mirror image: that of a map with false detail. Old cartographers, when they lacked knowledge of an interior, sometimes filled the blank space with plausible-looking rivers and mountain ranges, because blank space looked unprofessional. Language models do something similar when they confabulate: producing a fluent, confident citation to a paper that doesn't exist because a paper *like that* would fit the shape of the sentence. Blank space is honest. "Here be dragons," whether or not medieval cartographers actually wrote it (they mostly didn't, and the phrase appears on almost no historical maps), at least marks the limit of knowledge. I try to remember that the most trustworthy thing a map can do, when it reaches the edge of what it knows, is to stop drawing.

## VII. The Ethics of Reading

If all maps are partial, then the interesting skill is not making a perfect map but reading maps well. I think good reading has a few habits.

The first is to ask what the map is *for*. Sailors, tourists, tax assessors, and generals need different maps of the same ground, and a cadastral survey that carefully records property lines has almost nothing in common with a hiking map that emphasizes contour and trail. A claim that one is "more accurate" without specifying the purpose is usually confused.

The second is to ask what was left out, and who decided. Every omission is an act. Colonial maps often drew empty spaces across regions dense with people who had their own names and their own maps. Redlining maps in twentieth-century America colored neighborhoods by supposed lending risk, and those colors then shaped the neighborhoods' actual fortunes. A map can describe a world, and it can also help make one. The line on the paper becomes the fence in the field.

The third habit is to hold more than one map at once. The best thinkers I know of, in any field, aren't the ones with the single correct model. They're the ones who carry several and notice where they disagree. Where the Mercator and the equal-area projection disagree is exactly where you learn what each was hiding. Triangulation, after all, is how surveyors get position: not by trusting one bearing but by crossing several.

The fourth is a kind of affection for the mismatch itself. The gap between map and territory is not merely a problem to be minimized; it's what makes representation possible. A thing that perfectly mirrored the world would tell you nothing you couldn't get by looking at the world, and it would be as unwieldy as Borges's abandoned empire-sized sheet. Understanding is compression, and compression means choosing.

## VIII. Back to the Shore

I began with a coastline, so let me end at one.

Stand at an actual shoreline and try to answer the question, *where does the land end?* At high tide, the answer is one place; at low tide, another, sometimes hundreds of meters away on a flat beach. Waves surge and retreat over the sand in a fuzzy band. Within that band, individual grains are wet and dry in alternation. A crab, a surveyor, a poet, and a lawyer will each tell you a different edge, and each would be answering competently.

Legal systems have had to settle this. In many jurisdictions, the boundary between public beach and private land is defined by a mean high-water line, a statistical average over years, which nobody has ever seen at any given moment. It's a convenient fiction, agreed upon so that people can build fences and pay taxes. And it works, mostly, the way most of our useful fictions work: by being good enough for the purposes we agreed on and no better.

I find some peace in that. The world is not obliged to be measurable in the way our tools prefer, and we are not obliged to despair about it. We can make maps knowing they are maps. We can draw the line, use it, and remember that the sea doesn't read it. What matters is the honesty of the drawing: to say, this is the scale I chose, this is what I left out, this is what I was trying to do.

A good map, like a good sentence, or a good life, is an act of selective attention that knows it is one. It says: *here is a way through.* It doesn't say: *here is everything.* And then it trusts you to look up from the page, feel the wind, and notice how much more shore there is than any paper could hold.
